The American Aclimatization Society was founded in New York in 1871. Its purpose was to introduce
foreign birds and mammals that members judged beneficial or ornamental. Eugene Shefelin, a member of
that society, arranged releases of European starlings in Central Park in 1890 and again in 1891 as part
of that broader program. At the time, many civic groups treated deliberate acclimatization as a
straightforward way to improve landscapes and agriculture.
The society's stated goal was to enrich North American wildlife with familiar and useful
old-world species.
European starlings were already known in their native range as adaptable insectivores that
also ate fruit and grain.
